metadata.title: Circumventing construct-irrelevant variance in international assessments using cognitive diagnostic modeling: A curriculum-sensitive measure

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 1995 mathematics data with a reduced analytic sample restricted to educational systems with at least 60% valid teacher information at the classroom level and to students with complete teacher data for the MG-DINA estimation. The authors explicitly state that sampling weights were used to calculate country means for both the Tc statistic and the conventional IRT-based achievement scores, and they also report that the IRT-based ranking from the full sample and the reduced sample are highly correlated. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR or jackknife) is mentioned, so uncertainty quantification at the replicate level is not documented. Because the core scaling is based on cognitive diagnostic modeling (MG-DINA) and MAP skill estimation, the paper relies on the TIMSS complex-sampling weights for country-level comparisons rather than for within-model parameter estimation details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is drawn from TIMSS 1995 mathematics for secondary students (target population: 13-year-olds; seventh, eighth, and ninth graders in most countries). The authors include 19 relevant educational systems/countries after selecting those with at least 60% valid teacher information on the classroom level; the total included sample is 142,077 students. They then exclude students with missing teacher data for the DINA/MG-DINA estimation, reducing the effective sample size to 56,525. For MG-DINA conditional independence assumptions, they further exclude students who did not answer more than 20 questions (230 students excluded, 0.09% of the full sample). For the achievement-side comparison, they also exclude the same 1,327 students that were excluded in the official TIMSS international report due to missingness in the international study report, and they use the reduced sample for Tc and the IRT-based means.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 Grade 8 Mathematics (secondary; curriculum-sensitive Tc scaling)
main_findings.target_variable: Curriculum-sensitive performance statistic Tc (proportion of taught topics not learned)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Tc ranking across 19 countries: KOR Tc=0.29 (sd=0.09), HKG Tc=0.34 (0.17), BFL Tc=0.34 (0.15), SVK Tc=0.44 (0.11), CZE Tc=0.44 (0.12), BFR Tc=0.46 (0.11), CHE Tc=0.46 (0.16), AUS Tc=0.50 (0.17), PRT Tc=0.69 (0.08), IRN Tc=0.70 (0.12). Correlation between Tc-based ranking and IRT-based average achievement ranking: r = −0.95 (Fig. 2). Correlation between IRT-based ranking using full sample vs reduced Tc sample: r = 0.99.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 Grade 8 Mathematics (secondary) the study leveraged teacher-reported taught topics, the Q-matrix skill requirements, and student response completeness to compute the curriculum-sensitive statistic Tc, finding that country rankings based on Tc were highly consistent with conventional IRT-based rankings (r = −0.95) while still revealing curriculum mismatch patterns. This indicates that curriculum-sensitive scaling can preserve international ranking stability yet provide additional diagnostic information about which taught skills were not mastered, supporting more targeted curriculum and teaching interventions even when overall rank changes are small.

data.outcome_summary: The study develops and illustrates a curriculum-sensitive scaling approach for international achievement comparisons using TIMSS 1995 mathematics data from 19 educational systems (secondary students; target age 13). The method estimates binary skill mastery profiles with MG-DINA using a Q-matrix that maps items to 11 aggregated math skills, and it combines these skill posteriors with teacher survey reports of which topics were taught in each classroom to compute Tc: the average proportion of taught topics that were insufficiently understood. Country means and the Tc-based ranking are computed using sampling weights, and the authors compare Tc to conventional IRT-based average achievement using the TIMSS public-use scores. The Tc ranking shows strong alignment with the IRT ranking (r = −0.95) and the IRT ranking is nearly unchanged when moving from the full sample to the reduced teacher-complete sample (r = 0.99). Limitations include substantial missing teacher information requiring sample reduction and the possibility that teacher reports and the Q-matrix do not perfectly match the tested skills, which may attenuate ranking differences.
